warmup.q: Inside coroutineScope { }, you start val gravy = async { makeGravy() } and then do 500 ms of other work before calling gravy.await(). The gravy burns at 100 ms and throws. When does anything happen?
options: Only at await(), at 500 ms: until then the exception waits inside the Deferred
At 100 ms: the scope is cancelled, the other work stops, and coroutineScope throws
Never: an exception in async is ignored unless someone awaits it
At 100 ms the exception is printed by the uncaught handler, and await() returns null
warmup.why: A failed child cancels its parent at once, and that is as true for async as for launch. The exception waits in the Deferred only when the parent is a supervisor or there is no parent. Here the scope is cancelled at 100 ms and await() is never reached: the smell reaches the kitchen before anyone lifts the lid.

opening:
The gravy burns. Nobody in the kitchen has to be told: the smell reaches everyone at once. The cook takes the potatoes off the heat too, because the main course can't go out without gravy, and tells the family what happened. But by the window, three trays for tomorrow's bake sale are in the oven: cookies, scones and muffins. They have nothing to do with the gravy, and if the scones burn later, the cookies should still come out.

Coroutines face the same two cases. In Structured concurrency, a failure went up the tree and stopped the siblings. Cancellation and timeouts showed that a cancel is not a failure. Now the burnt dish itself: where does a coroutine's exception go, and who gets to hear it? The easy trap is to think an async keeps its failure under the lid until somebody calls await.

In this lesson, we'll watch launch and async report a failure, find where a handler really runs, let a supervisor keep one burnt tray from spoiling the rest, and spot the one-line fix that cuts a coroutine loose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with burnt gravy that the whole kitchen smelled at once, and a bake sale where one burnt tray shouldn't spoil the rest. A failed child tells its parent at once, from launch or async. The handler is the notebook for failures that reach the top. A supervisor lets children fail alone, and launch(SupervisorJob()) only looks like one.

Now search your own code for runCatching around await() inside coroutineScope, and for a Job passed to launch or async. Each one is error handling that runs too late, or not at all.

Next, we'll leave single results behind. How do you write code that hands back many values, one at a time, and does nothing until somebody asks?

sections.h: A burnt dish tells its parent at once, from launch and async alike
sections.html:
A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause and resume without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code. A coroutine that ends with an exception other than CancellationException has failed. (CancellationException, from the last lesson, means "cancelled", which is not a failure.) A failed child tells its parent at once. Every coroutine has a job, the handle to its life. With a regular job, the parent then does what Structured concurrency described: it cancels its other children, waits for them to stop, and fails with the same exception. A scope is what hands new coroutines their parent, and coroutineScope { } makes one that waits for every child started in it.

That much is true of launch. It surprises people that it's just as true of async. Builders called a Deferred a pot with the lid on, and it's natural to think a burnt dish stays under the lid until somebody lifts it with await. That is how a failed Java CompletableFuture behaves: it waits quietly for join. A coroutine doesn't:

Java
// Java equivalent: a failed future tells nobody until someone joins it
CompletableFuture<Gravy> gravy = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> makeGravy(), pool);
CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> roastPotatoes(), pool);
Thread.sleep(500);                      // passed: the potatoes keep roasting too
gravy.join();                           // the failure shows up only here
Kotlin
coroutineScope {
    val gravy = async { makeGravy() }   // throws BurnedException at 100 ms
    launch { roastPotatoes() }          // takes a second
    delay(500)                          // never passed: the scope is cancelled at 100 ms
    gravy.await()
}

Predict what prints, and when. AsyncFailsWithoutAwait, in the Try it below, runs exactly this, with BurnedException, an exception the demos define for a ruined dish:

  161 ms  potatoes: finally
  188 ms  caller caught: the gravy burned

The gravy burned at 100 ms (161 ms by the clock, on a JVM that had just started), the potatoes came off the heat, and the caller had the exception. The line the body would print at 500 ms never appeared. The smell reached the whole kitchen before anyone lifted the lid.

The Java twin is the honest contrast. Nothing reacts at 100 ms. The caller learns about the gravy only when it joins at 500 ms. The potatoes roast on to potatoes: done at 1,056 ms, because a future has no parent to tell.

The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 docs say it directly: async follows the same rules as launch. Only when the parent is a supervisor, or there is no parent, is the exception "only available through the returned Deferred". So a try around await doesn't protect the scope. By the time await would throw, the child has already cancelled everything around it. runCatching { gravy.await() } inside coroutineScope is a common bug, and it's one of the bugs in this lesson's lab.

Where do launch and async differ, then? Only when a failure has nobody above it to tell. A root coroutine is one with no parent coroutine above it. A root launch hands its exception to a handler, which the next section covers. A root async keeps it in the Deferred, and await rethrows it. That's the same split as execute and submit on a Java executor, a pool that runs submitted tasks. execute sends a task's exception to the thread's uncaught exception handler, the code that runs when an exception escapes a thread, while submit keeps it in the Future for get.

A failed child cancels its parent the moment it fails, from launch or async. Catching at await is too late.

So inside a tree, a failure always goes up. At the top of the tree, somebody has to write it down.

code.title: AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope /** The exception the demos of this lesson throw for a ruined dish. */ class BurnedException(message: String) : Exception(message) private var t0 = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { t0 = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" try { val mainCourse: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { val gravy = async { delay(100); throw BurnedException("the gravy burned") } // nobody awaits this yet launch { try { delay(1_000); log("potatoes: done") } finally { log("potatoes: finally") } } delay(500) log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to await the gravy") gravy.await() } if (supervised) supervisorScope(mainCourse) else coroutineScope(mainCourse) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: BurnedException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt: a failed CompletableFuture tells nobody. // The failure sits in the future until someone joins it, and the sibling task runs on. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava { static class BurnedException extends RuntimeException { BurnedException(String message) { super(message); } } static long T0; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { T0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture<Void> gravy = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); throw new BurnedException("the gravy burned"); // nobody joins this yet }, pool); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { try { sleep(1_000); log("potatoes: done"); } finally { log("potatoes: finally"); } }, pool); sleep(500); log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to join the gravy"); try { gravy.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { log("caller caught: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } } // close() waits for the potatoes, which nobody cancelled log("pool closed"); } }

try.expect: Plain: at about 100 ms, potatoes: finally and caller caught: the gravy burned (161 and 188 ms here, on a JVM that had just started). The body's 500 ms line never prints. With -Pargs=supervisor, the failed async does nothing on its own. The body prints at 500 ms, await rethrows, and because the block itself threw, supervisorScope cancels the potatoes (potatoes: finally) and rethrows. The Java twin is the contrast: nothing reacts at 100 ms, the caller sees the failure only when it joins at 500 ms, and the potatoes roast on to about 1,000 ms.

sections.h: The kitchen notebook: CoroutineExceptionHandler runs only for roots
sections.html:
Every kitchen has a notebook by the oven where someone writes down what went wrong: "scones burnt, oven runs hot". It helps next week. It does nothing for this week's scones.

CoroutineExceptionHandler is that notebook. It's a context element, one entry in the note clipped to every coroutine from Dispatchers and the coroutine context, and it receives the exceptions nobody else handled. By the time it runs, the coroutine has already finished, so there's nothing left to rescue. Use it to log and to count.

The rule that trips people up: only root coroutines use it. A child passes its exception to its parent, all the way to the top, so a handler on a child is never asked. A handler takes effect in two places. One is a coroutine launched straight into a scope you created yourself, such as CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + handler).launch { }, so that no coroutine sits above it. The other is a direct child of a supervisor, which handles its own failure the way a root does (next section). It never takes effect on async, which keeps its exception for await:

Java
// Java equivalent: the thread's uncaught handler sees execute() failures, never submit() ones
Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> log.warn("task failed on {}", t.getName(), e);
ExecutorService oven = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> {
    Thread t = new Thread(r, "oven");
    t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler);
    return t;
});
oven.execute(() -> { throw new BurnedException("the tray burned"); });   // the handler gets it
Kotlin
coroutineScope {
    launch(handler) { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") }   // ignored: this is a child
}                                                                  // coroutineScope throws

val oven = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler)
oven.launch { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") }            // a root: the handler gets it

HandlerOnlyAtRoot, in the Try it below, puts one handler in three places. Predict which of them reach the notebook. It printed:

1. handler on a child inside coroutineScope:
  coroutineScope threw: the tray burned  (the child's handler was ignored)
2. handler on a scope with a SupervisorJob, root launch:
  handler got: the tray burned (from root-launch)
3. the same scope, root async that nobody awaits:
  nothing printed: the failure waits in the Deferred
  await threw: the tray burned

Only the root launch reached the notebook. The child's handler was skipped, and the root async kept its burnt tray under the lid until await lifted it.

With no handler in the context, the library falls back to the JVM's last resort: the thread's uncaught exception handler, which usually prints a stack trace to the error output. A handler also ignores CancellationException, since a cancel isn't a failure. And when several children fail at once, the first exception wins, and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. Read the suppressed list before you decide only one thing went wrong.

In practice, put one handler on each long-lived scope you own, at the line where you create the scope. Don't sprinkle handlers on launch calls inside ordinary code, where a failure should reach the caller and a plain try around coroutineScope can deal with it.

A handler only records failures, and only for root coroutines. Put it on the scopes you own.

Case 2 used something we haven't explained yet: a SupervisorJob, a job that lets its children fail one at a time.

code.title: HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking fun main() = runBlocking { // the kitchen notebook: writes down what went wrong, after the fact val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> println(" handler got: ${e.message} (from ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name})") } println("1. handler on a child inside coroutineScope:") try { coroutineScope { launch(handler + CoroutineName("child")) { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") } } } catch (e: BurnedException) { println(" coroutineScope threw: ${e.message} (the child's handler was ignored)") } println("2. handler on a scope with a SupervisorJob, root launch:") val oven = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler) oven.launch(CoroutineName("root-launch")) { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") }.join() println("3. the same scope, root async that nobody awaits:") val d = oven.async(CoroutineName("root-async")) { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") } delay(100) println(" nothing printed: the failure waits in the Deferred") try { d.await() } catch (e: BurnedException) { println(" await threw: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: HandlerOnlyAtRootJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt: execute() sends a task's exception to the thread's // uncaught exception handler (like a root launch and its handler), while submit() keeps it // inside the Future until someone calls get() (like a root async and await). package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class HandlerOnlyAtRootJava { static class BurnedException extends RuntimeException { BurnedException(String message) { super(message); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler got: " + e.getMessage() + " (on " + t.getName() + ")"); ExecutorService oven = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "oven"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler); return t; }); Runnable failing = () -> { throw new BurnedException("the tray burned"); }; System.out.println("1. execute(): the exception reaches the thread's handler"); oven.execute(failing); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println("2. submit() that nobody waits for:"); Future<?> f = oven.submit(failing); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(" nothing printed: the failure waits in the Future"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" get threw: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } oven.shutdown(); oven.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: Only case 2 prints handler got: the tray burned (from root-launch). In case 1 the handler on the child is ignored and coroutineScope throws. In case 3 nothing prints until await rethrows. After your change, case 1 prints handler got too: a direct child of supervisorScope handles its own failure like a root, and the scope returns normally. The Java twin shows the same split: execute reaches the thread's handler, and submit keeps the failure in the Future until get.

sections.h: A supervisor lets one tray burn without stopping the others
sections.html:
Back to the trays by the window. The cookies, scones and muffins for the bake sale share an oven, but they don't need each other: if the scones burn, the other two should still come out. Structured concurrency made a promise about exactly this. Its Oven class had a plain Job, so one burnt tray switched the whole oven off. Lesson 6 was to swap it for a SupervisorJob, "so one burned tray doesn't spoil the rest". It also pictured a reminder sent by text, by email and by phone, where any one of them is enough. Both are supervisor work.

A supervisor is a job whose children fail independently. A child's failure doesn't cancel its siblings or the supervisor. Cancellation still flows down, so cancelling the supervisor still cancels every child.

There are two ways to get one. supervisorScope { } is the supervisor version of coroutineScope, for work the caller waits for. Here it bakes every tray of one order and reports how each went:

Java
// Java equivalent: futures are independent, so each one handles its own failure
Map<Tray, CompletableFuture<Outcome>> trays = new EnumMap<>(Tray.class);
bakers.forEach((tray, baker) -> trays.put(tray, CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> baker.bake(order), pool)
    .handle((ok, e) -> e == null ? new Baked() : new Failed(e.getMessage()))));
CompletableFuture.allOf(trays.values().toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
Kotlin
suspend fun bakeAll(order: String): Map<Tray, Outcome> = supervisorScope {
    val trays = bakers.mapValues { (_, baker) -> async { baker.bake(order) } }
    trays.mapValues { (_, tray) ->
        try { tray.await(); Outcome.Baked }
        catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
        catch (e: Exception) { Outcome.Failed(e.message ?: e.toString()) }
    }
}

With async children, each failure stays in its Deferred, and await rethrows it where you can catch it. That's why the try around await works here, when it was too late in the first section. With launch children there's no await, so the failure goes to the handler in the context. supervisorScope doesn't install a handler of its own.

SupervisorDemo, in the Try it below, puts three trays in at once. The cookies take 300 ms, the muffins 100 ms, and the scones burn at 50 ms. First under coroutineScope:

  100 ms  cookies: finally
  125 ms  muffins: finally
  131 ms  caller caught: the scones burned

One burnt tray, and the oven was emptied. Now with -Pargs=supervisor:

  104 ms  handler: the scones burned
  148 ms  muffins baked
  148 ms  muffins: finally
  342 ms  cookies baked
  343 ms  cookies: finally
  344 ms  scope returned normally

The notebook got the scones, and the other two trays came out on time. (Every line is about 50 ms late, because the JVM had just started and the machine was busy.)

SupervisorJob() is the supervisor for a scope you own, the long-lived kind from Structured concurrency: CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler). Every launch into that scope is a child that can fail alone, and its failure goes to the scope's handler. The lab gives the Oven exactly that.

One rule doesn't change. If the body of supervisorScope itself throws, the whole scope is cancelled, children included. A supervisor protects the children from each other, not from a failing block. That's why the first section's demo, run with -Pargs=supervisor, still took the potatoes off the heat when await rethrew.

Here the kitchen picture breaks a little. A real cook decides about each burnt dish as it happens. A scope decides once, when you create it: every child of a supervisor fails alone, and every child of a plain job takes its siblings down. So pick per piece of work. A course that needs all its dishes wants coroutineScope. Trays for a bake sale, reminders on three channels and other independent extras want a supervisor.

When siblings need each other, use coroutineScope. When they don't, use a supervisor.

So a supervisor goes around the children, or into a scope's constructor. There's a third place people put it, and it's the wrong one.

code.title: SupervisorDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope private var started = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg)) // supervisorScope installs no handler of its own, so failed launch children need one in the context private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log("handler: ${e.message}") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking(handler) { started = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" // three trays for the bake sale, all in the oven at once val bakeAll: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { launch { try { delay(300); log("cookies baked") } finally { log("cookies: finally") } } launch { delay(50); throw BurnedException("the scones burned") } launch { try { delay(100); log("muffins baked") } finally { log("muffins: finally") } } } try { if (supervised) supervisorScope(bakeAll) else coroutineScope(bakeAll) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: BurnedException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: SupervisorDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SupervisorDemo.kt: CompletableFutures are independent by default, like // children of a supervisor. Nothing cancels the siblings, so each future handles its own failure. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class SupervisorDemoJava { static class BurnedException extends RuntimeException { BurnedException(String message) { super(message); } } static long started; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { started = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { // three trays for the bake sale, all in the oven at once CompletableFuture<Void> cookies = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(300); log("cookies baked"); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> scones = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(50); throw new BurnedException("the scones burned"); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> muffins = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); log("muffins baked"); }, pool); // each failure is handled where it happens; the siblings never hear about it CompletableFuture<Void> sconesHandled = scones.exceptionally(e -> { log("handled: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); return null; }); CompletableFuture.allOf(cookies, sconesHandled, muffins).join(); log("all three trays are out"); } } }

try.expect: With coroutineScope, the cookies and muffins are cancelled within about 50 ms of the scones burning (their finally lines) and the caller catches the scones burned. With -Pargs=supervisor, the handler prints at about 50 ms, the muffins are baked at about 100 ms and the cookies at about 300 ms, and the scope returns normally (each line runs some 50 ms late on a busy machine). The Java twin behaves like the supervisor without being asked: futures are independent, so each one has to handle its own failure.

video.title: A burnt dish tells its parent at once, from launch or async alike; a supervisor keeps one burnt tray from spoiling the rest, the handler is the notebook by the oven for failures at the top, and launch(SupervisorJob()) cuts the child out of the tree

sections.h: launch(SupervisorJob()) looks supervised but cuts the child loose
sections.html:
Here is the most common wrong fix. A dinner has a dessert in the oven, and every time the dessert burns, it takes the main course down with it. So someone writes:

Java
// Java equivalent: hand the task to some other, longer-lived executor
try (var dinner = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> bakeDessert());    // no longer part of this dinner
    dinner.submit(() -> cookMainCourse());
}
Kotlin
coroutineScope {
    launch(SupervisorJob()) { bakeDessert() }   // meant as "make this child supervised"
    launch { cookMainCourse() }
}

It reads like "a supervised child", and it is something else. A builder's context argument overrides the scope's, as Dispatchers and the coroutine context showed, and that includes the Job. So the new coroutine becomes the child of that fresh SupervisorJob, which has no parent of its own. The dessert has left the tree. coroutineScope doesn't wait for it, cancelling the dinner doesn't cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler or the uncaught exception handler instead of to the dinner. It's GlobalScope from Structured concurrency, wearing a new apron.

SupervisorTrap, in the Try it below, starts one child each way and cancels the dinner at 100 ms:

  120 ms  normal child: finally
  165 ms  dinner cancelled and joined
  324 ms  trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me
  566 ms  main done

The dinner was cancelled and joined. A good 150 ms later, the trap child was still at work.

The compiler now says so too. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates the overload of launch that takes a Job. Compiling the demo prints a warning that begins: "Passing a Job to coroutine builders breaks structured concurrency, leading to hard-to-diagnose errors." The same rule applies to async and withContext, with one documented exception: withContext(NonCancellable) for cleanup, from the last lesson.

Put the supervisor where it belongs. Inside a function, wrap the children in supervisorScope { }. For background work, give the owning class a scope built with SupervisorJob() in its constructor, and launch into it. Then the work is supervised and still owned: the scope waits for it, counts it and cancels it when the owner's life ends.

Never pass a Job to a builder. Put the supervisor in a scope instead.

When you see launch(SupervisorJob()), launch(Job()) or async(SupervisorJob()) in a review, ask what the author wanted. The answer is almost always one of those two shapes.

try.title: Cancel the dinner and watch the trap child carry on
steps: Read SupervisorTrap.kt. The dinner is cancelled at 100 ms. Predict which of the two children prints after that.
Run it. Look for the deprecation warning in the Gradle output when the demo compiles.
Delete SupervisorJob() from the first launch and run it again.
Run the Java twin, where the detached task lives on a shared executor.

code.title: SupervisorTrap.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var since = 0L private fun stamp(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main() = runBlocking { since = System.nanoTime() val dinner = launch { // looks like "a supervised child". It is a child of a brand-new SupervisorJob instead, // so it has left the dinner's tree: nobody waits for it and nobody cancels it. launch(SupervisorJob()) { delay(300) stamp("trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me") } launch { try { delay(300); stamp("normal child: done") } finally { stamp("normal child: finally") } } } delay(100) dinner.cancelAndJoin() stamp("dinner cancelled and joined") delay(400) stamp("main done") }

alt.title: SupervisorTrapJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SupervisorTrap.kt: a task sent to some other executor is not part of the // dinner. Shutting the dinner's executor down interrupts its own tasks, not that one. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SupervisorTrapJava { static long since; static void stamp(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { since = System.nanoTime(); ExecutorService shared = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // what launch(SupervisorJob()) amounts to ExecutorService dinner = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); shared.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("detached task: still running, nobody cancelled me"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("detached task: interrupted"); } }); dinner.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("dinner task: done"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("dinner task: interrupted"); } }); Thread.sleep(100); dinner.shutdownNow(); dinner.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); stamp("dinner cancelled and joined"); Thread.sleep(400); shared.shutdown(); stamp("main done"); } }

try.expect: The normal child's finally runs at about 100 ms, and the dinner is cancelled and joined. Then, at about 300 ms, trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me prints: it was never part of the dinner's tree. After your change, neither child prints after the cancel. The Java twin shows the same leak with a task on a shared pool. (The warning appears only when the file compiles; once the class is compiled, Gradle doesn't print it again.)

refs.title: launch (API reference: why not to pass a Job)

compare.title: A background sender: pool with an uncaught handler vs supervisor scope with a handler

java.title: ReminderSender.java
java.html: class ReminderSender implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "reminders"); // last resort for task failures, like a CoroutineExceptionHandler t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("reminder failed", e)); return t; }); void remind(String guest) { pool.execute(() -> texts.send(guest)); // execute, not submit: failures reach the handler } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } }

kotlin.title: ReminderSender.kt
kotlin.html: class ReminderSender(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("reminder failed", e) } // SupervisorJob: one failed text doesn't cancel the others or the scope private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun remind(guest: String): Job = scope.launch { texts.send(guest) } // a root child: failures reach the handler fun close() = scope.cancel() }

compare.note: The two defaults are opposite. A Java thread pool is a supervisor without being asked: tasks never cancel each other, so your only job is to make sure failures are seen (execute sends them to the uncaught handler, submit hides them in a Future nobody reads). A coroutine scope with a plain Job fails together, which is right for a course of dishes and wrong for a background sender, so you opt in with SupervisorJob(). After that the shapes match: launch is execute and goes to the handler, async is submit and keeps its failure for await. What Kotlin adds is the tree. The scope still knows every child, so close() cancels the texts in flight, and a test that calls remind can wait for them.

steps.say: A family recipe app serves a dinner: it marks the dinner as cooked in the recipe book, then posts a photo to the family chat. The chat was down one evening, the photo's failure cancelled the recipe-book entry, and someone fixed it like this. Since then the tests are flaky (photos post after a test has ended), and the app tries to post photos after it has closed. Why?
steps.code: suspend fun serveDinner(menu: Menu) = coroutineScope { val dinner = kitchen.cook(menu) launch { recipeBook.record(dinner) } launch(SupervisorJob()) { chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo) } // the "fix" dinner }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same fix: the photo goes to a shared pool nobody owns Dinner serveDinner(Menu menu) throws Exception { Dinner dinner = kitchen.cook(menu); try (var request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { request.submit(() -> recipeBook.record(dinner)); SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo())); // the "fix" } return dinner; }

steps.say: The SupervisorJob() became the photo's parent, so the photo left the dinner's tree: nothing waits for it and nothing cancels it. Decide what the author wanted. Serving dinner shouldn't wait for the chat, so the photo belongs to a long-lived owner. Give that owner a supervisor scope and a handler.
steps.code: class PhotoPoster(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) : AutoCloseable { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> log.warn("photo ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name} not posted", e) // 1. log with the dinner's name } // 2. supervised and owned: children fail alone, close() still reaches them private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun post(dinner: Dinner): Job = scope.launch(CoroutineName(dinner.name)) { chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the poster owns its pool and its failure handler class PhotoPoster implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "photos"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("photo not posted", e)); // 1. log return t; }); // 2. owned: close() reaches every task void post(Dinner dinner) { pool.execute(() -> chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo())); } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } }

steps.say: The dinner goes back to plain structured code. The recipe-book entry must succeed or fail with the dinner, so it stays part of the call. The photo is handed to its owner.
steps.code: suspend fun serveDinner(menu: Menu): Dinner { val dinner = kitchen.cook(menu) recipeBook.record(dinner) // 3. part of the dinner: a failure fails the dinner photoPoster.post(dinner) // handed off: the owner deals with failures return dinner }

alt.html: Dinner serveDinner(Menu menu) { Dinner dinner = kitchen.cook(menu); recipeBook.record(dinner); // 3. part of the dinner photoPoster.post(dinner); // handed off to its owner return dinner; }

steps.say: If the app must also show whether the photo got through, the dinner does wait for it, and the right shape is supervisorScope with an outcome for the call instead.
steps.code: suspend fun serveAndShare(menu: Menu): Pair<Dinner, Boolean> = supervisorScope { val dinner = kitchen.cook(menu) recipeBook.record(dinner) // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone val photo = async { chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo) } val posted = try { photo.await(); true } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { false } dinner to posted }

alt.html: Map.Entry<Dinner, Boolean> serveAndShare(Menu menu) { Dinner dinner = kitchen.cook(menu); recipeBook.record(dinner); // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone boolean posted = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo()), pool) .handle((ok, e) -> e == null) .join(); return Map.entry(dinner, posted); }

steps.say: Self-check: in step 4, recipeBook.record throws. What happens to the photo? (Nothing: it hasn't started yet. The exception is thrown by the supervisorScope block itself, so the scope is cancelled and rethrows. A supervisor protects siblings from each other, not from a failing block.)

lab.title: An oven where one burnt tray doesn't spoil the rest
steps: Meet the code. Trays.kt holds the shared model: the three trays of a bake-sale order, a Baker that bakes one tray (and throws BurnedException if it burns), and the Outcome of each tray. bakeAll bakes every tray of one order while the caller waits. Oven is the background oven from Structured concurrency, which bakes trays until it's switched off. Run the tests: five of eight fail.
In BakeAll.kt, switch coroutineScope to supervisorScope, so a burnt tray stays in its own Deferred.
Give each tray its own deadline with withTimeoutOrNull(timeout) inside the async, and map a null result to Outcome.Failed("timed out").
Replace runCatching around await() with a try that rethrows CancellationException and turns any other exception into Outcome.Failed(message). The four bakeAll tests should now pass.
In Oven.kt, build the scope from dispatcher + SupervisorJob() + handler, where the handler calls reportBurned with the tray's name from the coroutine's CoroutineName.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then try launch(SupervisorJob() + ...) in put instead, and see which tests catch it.
hints: withTimeoutOrNull(timeout) { baker.bake(order) } returns Unit when the tray is done and null when it times out.
CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, error -> ... } gets the failed coroutine's context, so context[CoroutineName]?.name is the tray name that put set.
A handler is used only by root coroutines. Children launched straight into a scope built with SupervisorJob() count as roots, so a handler in the scope's context sees their failures.
The switchOff test already passes on the stub. It is there to catch the launch(SupervisorJob()) trap.

drill.title: A supervised background worker from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class ThankYouTexter(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) with fun thank(guest: String): Job, which calls a suspending texts.send(guest) in the background. One failed text must not stop the others, every failure is logged with log.warn, and suspend fun close() cancels the texts still pending and waits for them.

answer.html: class ThankYouTexter(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("thank-you text failed", e) } private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun thank(guest: String): Job = scope.launch { texts.send(guest) } suspend fun close() { scope.coroutineContext.job.cancelAndJoin() } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a pool is independent by default; route failures to a handler class ThankYouTexter implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "thank-you"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("thank-you text failed", e)); return t; }); void thank(String guest) { pool.execute(() -> texts.send(guest)); } @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdownNow(); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

recap: A failed child cancels its parent at once, whether it was started with launch or async, and whether or not anyone awaits it.
launch and async differ only at the root: a root launch goes to a CoroutineExceptionHandler, a root async keeps the exception for await.
CoroutineExceptionHandler runs only for root coroutines and direct children of a supervisor, never for async. It records failures; it can't rescue anything.
A supervisor lets children fail alone, while cancellation still flows down. Use supervisorScope inside a function and SupervisorJob() in the constructor of a scope you own.
launch(SupervisorJob()) replaces the parent and cuts the child out of the tree. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates passing a Job to builders.
The limit: a supervisor protects siblings from each other, not from the block that started them. If the block itself throws, everything under it is cancelled.

explain.prompt: A friend asks why their runCatching { tray.await() } inside coroutineScope didn't stop one burnt tray from failing the whole bake, and why moving a CoroutineExceptionHandler onto the async didn't help either. Explain, and say what you would write instead.
explain.answer: In a regular coroutineScope, a child that fails tells its parent straight away, whether it's a launch or an async and whether or not anyone has awaited it. So the moment the tray burned, the scope was cancelled, the other trays were cancelled, and coroutineScope rethrew the exception. The runCatching around await came too late to matter. The handler did nothing because handlers only run for root coroutines, and an async never uses one anyway: it keeps its exception for await. If one burnt tray should not spoil the others, use supervisorScope. There, a failed async child just keeps its exception in its Deferred, so a try around each await, rethrowing CancellationException, turns each tray into a result or a failure. If the bake really needs every tray, keep coroutineScope and catch the exception around the whole scope instead.

deeper.html:
SupervisorJob(parent) takes an optional parent, and that link works in one direction. If the parent is cancelled or fails, the supervisor is cancelled with it. A failure of one of the supervisor's children doesn't travel up. That makes CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob(appJob) + dispatcher) a good shape for one part of a program that should stop with the whole program but never take it down.

supervisorScope and SupervisorJob differ in one detail that bites in tests. supervisorScope waits for all its children, like coroutineScope, and rethrows if its own block throws. A scope built with SupervisorJob() never completes on its own: it's a long-lived container, and you end it with cancel(). That's why the lab's Oven has an explicit switchOff().

The last-resort path on the JVM can be extended. kotlinx.coroutines looks up CoroutineExceptionHandler implementations through ServiceLoader, the JDK's mechanism for finding plug-in implementations on the classpath, and calls each of them before the thread's uncaught exception handler. kotlinx-coroutines-test uses that hook to collect exceptions from coroutines that escape a test, and since 1.7 runTest fails at the end if any were collected, even from coroutines that are not children of the test. That's why the lab's starting code fails loudly instead of printing a stack trace and passing.

Finally, CancellationException once more. Since a cancel isn't a failure, it never goes to a handler, and a child that ends with it never cancels its parent. That's the rule that made the runCatching loop in lesson 5 of this track so dangerous, and it's also why withTimeout inside a launch fails quietly. Code that turns a timeout into a real error (withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out")) produces an IllegalStateException, which does travel up the tree.
